title: Coordinate Precision Tool: Decimal Places
description: Control how many decimal places you keep when copying coordinates with the Coordinate Precision Tool — matched to real accuracy. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a phone fix honest to about 5 metres deserves 5 decimals (1.1 m grain) — the 8th decimal your app displays is measuring the table your phone sits on, not the world.

Mixed-precision columns look sloppy and join badly. Normalise the column's dress to its least-accurate member's honesty.
Coordinates in prose should carry the precision the method earned — typically 5 for GPS fieldwork, 4 for map-read points.
4 places ≈ 11 m, 5 ≈ 1.1 m, 6 ≈ 0.11 m (latitude grain, computed). Choosing 6 for a handheld GPS fix overclaims by two orders of magnitude — the ladder makes the overclaim visible.
Cutting digits (truncation) biases every point one way; rounding is neutral. This tool rounds — a small professionalism with systematic consequences at scale.

faq: How many decimals should I keep?
One more than your accuracy earns: phone fixes 5, map clicks 4, survey kit 6. The table on this page prices each place in metres — choose with it open.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — precision choices are datum-independent, but the pair being trimmed is assumed WGS84 like the rest of this family.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — the site's standing answer, quantified here: places set the grain of the claim, the source sets its truth.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Yes — trimmed pairs paste anywhere decimals do.
Rounding or truncation?
Rounding — truncation systematically drags points southwest (northeast in southern/eastern sign terms), a bias invisible per-point and obvious per-dataset.
The form wants exactly N places.
Set N here and copy the dressed value — trailing zeros included, which is what 'exactly N' usually means.
Privacy fuzzing?
Dropping to 3 or 2 places is the standard deliberate fuzz for sensitive locations — size it with the grain table so the fuzz matches the intent.
Longitude grain differs?
Yes — finer by the cosine of latitude. The table quotes latitude (the conservative axis); your longitude grain at 60° is half the table's.
Negative zero and edge dress?
Rounded outputs normalise cosmetic oddities (−0.0000 becomes 0.0000) — parsers downstream appreciate it.
Batch trimming?
One pair at a time here; the rounding tool is its sibling for quick jobs, and scripts wear the bulk work.
Should I store full precision anyway?
Store the fullest honest value; dress copies for use. Storage precision is cheap — false display precision is the sin, not the digits themselves.
